Neonatal specimens of Raja radula, the Rough skate, are infrequently encountered in trawl surveys, but the smallest free-swimming individual captured in the Mediterranean measured 13.5 cm in total length. Back-calculations from size-at-age relationships and observations of yolk-sac resorption indicate that the total length at birth is approximately 10 cm [Lb = approximately 10 cm], a value consistent with the relatively small size of the egg cases produced by this species. This modest starting length contrasts markedly with the dimensions attained by adult females. Extensive sampling efforts off the coasts of Tunisia and Greece have documented that female Rough skates reach a maximum total length of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the rajiform community in the region. Males, by comparison, rarely exceed 65 cm in total length. The ultimate wet weight for females can reach as high as 3.7 kilograms [Wwi = 3.7 kilograms], though such heavy individuals are seldom recorded and likely represent old, reproductively active adults with substantial energy reserves.

Sexual maturation in male Rough skates occurs at a notably smaller body size than in females. Field studies based on clasper calcification and gonadal histology have established that the total length at puberty for males is 47 cm [Lp = 47 cm], a threshold that is typically crossed during the third or fourth year of life. Females, which follow a slower growth trajectory and allocate more resources to somatic expansion before reproducing, attain female puberty at a total length of 56.5 cm [Lp = 56.5 cm]. This sex-specific divergence in maturation size is common among elasmobranchs and is generally interpreted as a reflection of the greater energetic demands imposed on gravid females during gestation and parturition. The delay in female maturation allows for the accumulation of sufficient body mass and lipid stores to support the development of multiple large, well-yolked ova and to sustain the subsequent brooding period.

Reproductive output in the Rough skate has been characterized through long-term captive observations and egg-case collections from the wild. When maintained in controlled experimental conditions at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females deposit between 80 and 154 egg cases per year. Each egg case contains a single fertilised ovum [N_R_i = Each egg case contains a single fertilised ovum], and females lay 80 to 154 eggs annually [Ri = 80 to 154 eggs annually], which translates into 80 to 154 egg cases per year [Ri = 80 to 154 egg cases per year]. This level of reproductive output is relatively modest for a skate of its size and aligns with a life-history strategy that prioritises the production of large, well-provisioned offspring over high fecundity. The consistency of laying across the year, rather than in strongly pulsed seasonal events, suggests a continuous or prolonged breeding period under favourable thermal conditions.

The ontogenetic schedule of Raja radula is characterised by a protracted embryonic phase and a slow pace of life. In captivity at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth, defined here as the interval from oviposition to hatching of the yolk-dependent embryo from its egg case, is approximately 6 months [ab = approximately 6 months]. This extended incubation period, exceeding that of many small-bodied skates, is likely linked to the relatively large size of the egg case and the substantial yolk reserves required to support embryonic development to an advanced state of organogenesis. Upon emergence, the neonate is fully formed and capable of immediate benthic foraging, though the early juvenile period remains a phase of elevated natural mortality. The prolonged developmental timeline sets a foundation for the species’ overall slow maturation and extended reproductive schedule.

Longevity records for the Rough skate are derived from mark-recapture programmes and captive maintenance studies conducted at temperatures approximating those of its native habitat. Under such conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum lifespan has been estimated at 12 years [am = 12 years]. This lifespan, while not exceptional among rajid skates, is sufficient to allow multiple reproductive cycles given the delayed onset of female maturity at 56.5 cm total length. The combination of a 6-month incubation period (approximately 6 months) [ab = approximately 6 months], a moderate annual fecundity of 80 to 154 eggs [Ri = annual fecundity of 80 to 154 eggs], and a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] positions Raja radula as a typical k-selected elasmobranch, with a life history that is sensitive to fishing pressure and environmental change at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Continued monitoring of these demographic parameters is essential for effective conservation planning in the Mediterranean basin.
